claims.text: The starting catalyst is a nearly equiatomic, multi-element alloy with low platinum-group-metal content.
A combined N-doping and dealloying treatment will generate a Pt-rich surface shell.
Exposure to a nitrogen-containing atmosphere can incorporate nitrogen while selectively removing non-Pt elements.
The treatment will form a Pt-rich shell on an N-doped high-entropy-alloy substrate.
N-doping alters the electronic structure of Pt sites.
The N-induced electronic-structure change improves oxygen adsorption.
The N-induced electronic-structure change improves reaction kinetics.
Dealloying selectively removes less-active elements and creates a Pt-enriched outer layer.
The Pt-enriched outer layer is more resistant to catalyst poisoning.
The Pt-enriched outer layer is more resistant to sintering.
The treated surface is more resistant to degradation caused by H2O, NO, and thermal stress.
The treated catalyst will have higher catalytic activity than the untreated catalyst under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The treated catalyst will retain activity longer and exhibit greater durability than the untreated catalyst after thermal aging and cycling.
The proposed treatment will maintain low platinum consumption despite forming a Pt-rich shell.
The benefits are expected within typical transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operating ranges.
Excessive temperature spikes or atypical pollutant loads may eliminate the expected benefits.
